oblivion

uh-BLIV-ee-un · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Oblivion is the state of being completely forgotten or no longer existing.

Once a household name, the once-popular soft drink brand slowly faded into oblivion after the company stopped advertising it.

Example

Historians say hundreds of ancient languages have already vanished into oblivion, with no living speakers left to remember them.

Oblivion describes total, permanent forgetting or disappearance -- not just a temporary dip in popularity.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

obscurity: Obscurity is the state of being little known or noticed -- an obscure poet still exists, still writes, and can still be rediscovered. Oblivion goes further: the thing is wiped from memory entirely, as if it had never existed at all.

nonexistence: Nonexistence is the plain fact of not existing, with no story attached to it. Oblivion is about memory: something slips into oblivion when the world forgets it completely -- it may even survive somewhere, unnoticed and unrecalled, which nonexistence never allows.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fame: the state of being widely known and recognized

permanence: the quality of lasting forever, without disappearing

Where it sits · how completely something fades away

neglect → oblivion → extinction

neglect vs. oblivion: Neglect is only a lack of attention or care -- much milder than oblivion, since a neglected statue still stands and a few people still remember it.

extinction vs. oblivion: Extinction is the complete and permanent disappearance of an entire species or type, even more final than oblivion.

Build the Word

The pieces

root (historical) — oblivi-: forgetting -- this root doesn't survive as its own standalone English word, but it shows up in the common adjective oblivious (Latin oblivisci, 'to forget')

suffix — -ion: the act, process, or result of (here, the state resulting from that act) (Latin)

Put it together: Oblivion comes from Latin oblivisci ('to forget'). The root doesn't survive on its own in English, but it lives on in the common word oblivious -- someone who is oblivious has, in a sense, forgotten to notice what's right in front of them.

Use the root in a new word: oblivious: He was so absorbed in his phone that he was completely oblivious to the fire alarm going off around him.

Word Building

Word Choice

Oblivion most often appears in the fixed phrases 'fall into oblivion' or 'fade into oblivion' -- describing something (a memory, a trend, a civilization) becoming completely forgotten or extinct.
